metadata.title: Operating Systems MCQ Quiz
metadata.description: 100 multiple-choice questions covering OS types, kernels and system calls, processes and threads, CPU scheduling, synchronization, deadlocks, memory management, virtual memory and file systems. Derived one-to-one from the Operating Systems Learn question bank.

questions.question: What is an operating system?
options: An application that runs on top of the hardware without special privileges
System software sitting between applications and hardware, managing processes, memory, files, devices, storage, security and the user interface
A compiler that translates source code into machine instructions
A firmware routine that only runs at machine startup
questions.explanation: The OS exists so programs never talk to hardware directly — it owns and arbitrates every resource.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid category of operating system?
options: Compiled, interpreted and hybrid systems
Static, dynamic and virtual systems
Batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, multiprocessing, distributed, network, real-time and embedded
Primary, secondary and tertiary systems
questions.explanation: The categories describe how jobs are admitted and scheduled, and how many machines or CPUs cooperate.

questions.question: What is the difference between hard and soft real-time systems?
options: Hard real-time runs on dedicated hardware while soft real-time runs on general-purpose machines
Hard real-time is simply faster on average than soft real-time
Soft real-time guarantees deadlines while hard real-time does not
In hard real-time, missing a deadline is a system failure (pacemakers, airbags); in soft real-time, missing one degrades quality but is tolerable (video streaming, VoIP)
questions.explanation: An RTOS guarantees a response within a strict time bound, not merely good average performance.

questions.question: What is the main objective of multiprogramming?
options: Maximizing CPU utilization and throughput by switching to another job whenever one blocks on I/O
Guaranteeing each user a fixed time slice for interactivity
Running the same program on several CPUs simultaneously
Reducing the memory footprint of each individual process
questions.explanation: Several jobs are kept in main memory so the CPU never sits idle waiting for a slow device.

questions.question: What distinguishes multiprocessing from multithreading?
options: Multiprocessing splits one process into threads while multithreading uses several CPUs
Multiprocessing means more than one physical CPU or core executing simultaneously; multithreading means one process split into several threads that share its memory
Both refer to running multiple programs on a single CPU
Multithreading requires multiple machines while multiprocessing does not
questions.explanation: Multiprogramming and multitasking are about scheduling, multiprocessing is about hardware, and multithreading is about program structure.

questions.question: What does a time-sharing system optimize for?
options: Raw throughput, by running each job to completion
Memory efficiency, by keeping only one process resident
Response time — the CPU switches between users every few milliseconds so each feels they have the machine to themselves
Power consumption, by idling the CPU between jobs
questions.explanation: Time-sharing needs preemptive scheduling and a short time quantum, trading some throughput for interactivity.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of a batch operating system?
options: It cannot execute more than one job in a day
It requires expensive multiprocessor hardware
It cannot store output on disk
No interactivity, hard debugging, the CPU sits idle during I/O, and one long job starves the rest
questions.explanation: Batch systems group similar jobs and run them without user interaction, which gives high throughput on long jobs but no responsiveness.

questions.question: What is spooling?
options: Buffering output for a slow device to disk first so the device consumes it at its own pace, letting the CPU and device overlap
Compressing data before writing it to disk
Copying a process from memory to swap space
Scheduling jobs in order of shortest execution time
questions.explanation: Simultaneous Peripheral Operation On-Line. The printer queue is the classic example — your process finishes immediately instead of blocking.

questions.question: What does the bootstrap program do?
options: It schedules which process runs after every timer interrupt
It stores the file system metadata on disk
It runs from ROM at power-on: performs hardware diagnostics, initializes devices, then loads the OS kernel into RAM and transfers control to it
It translates system calls into hardware instructions
questions.explanation: The bootloader is the bridge between firmware and the operating system, running before any OS code exists in memory.

questions.question: What characterizes Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP)?
options: One master CPU controls the system and assigns work to slave CPUs
Each CPU has its own local memory that it accesses faster than another CPU's memory
Only one CPU may execute kernel code at any time
All CPUs are peers sharing one main memory, and any CPU can run any task including kernel code
questions.explanation: AMP uses a master/slave arrangement; NUMA gives each CPU faster local memory, so the scheduler must keep a process near its own memory.

questions.question: What is the kernel?
options: The core of the OS, always resident in memory and running in privileged mode, managing processes, memory, drivers, file systems and system calls
The command-line interface a user types into
The set of utility programs shipped alongside the OS
The firmware stored in ROM that starts the machine
questions.explanation: The kernel is the only layer permitted to touch hardware directly — everything else must request it via a system call.

questions.question: How does the kernel differ from the operating system?
options: They are exactly the same thing
The kernel is one component — the resident core managing hardware and resources; the OS is the whole package including shell, utilities, libraries and GUI
The OS is a subset of the kernel
The kernel runs in user mode while the OS runs in kernel mode
questions.explanation: Every OS has a kernel, but a kernel alone is not a usable operating system.

questions.question: What is the trade-off between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
options: Microkernels are faster because they run everything in kernel space
Monolithic kernels are more stable because each driver is isolated

Monolithic keeps all services in kernel space — fast because calls are simple function calls, but one driver bug can crash the system; microkernel keeps only the minimum in kernel space with the rest as user-space servers — more stable and modular but slower due to message passing
There is no performance difference; the distinction is purely historical
questions.explanation: Linux and Unix are monolithic; QNX and Mach are microkernels; Windows NT is a hybrid.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shell and a kernel?
options: The shell manages hardware while the kernel accepts user commands
Both are equivalent interfaces to the hardware
The kernel is a replaceable user-space program while the shell is not
The shell is the outer interface (CLI or GUI) that reads commands and asks the kernel to carry them out; the kernel does the actual work on the hardware
questions.explanation: The shell is a replaceable user-space program — you can swap bash for zsh. The kernel is not replaceable while the system runs.

questions.question: Why are system calls necessary?
options: Because user code cannot touch hardware directly, so a system call is the only controlled door into the kernel for privileged operations
Because they run faster than ordinary function calls
Because the compiler cannot generate machine code for I/O operations
Because every program must register itself with the OS before running
questions.explanation: Categories: process control (fork, exec, exit, wait), file management (open, read, write, close), device management, information maintenance and communication.

questions.question: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
options: User mode has access to all instructions while kernel mode is restricted
In user mode a process can only run non-privileged instructions and access its own memory; in kernel mode all instructions and all memory are available, with a CPU mode bit tracking which is active
The two modes differ only in scheduling priority
Kernel mode is used only during system startup
questions.explanation: A system call, interrupt or trap flips the CPU into kernel mode and returning flips it back. This separation stops one buggy program taking down the machine.

questions.question: How does a library call differ from a system call?
options: A library call always crosses into the kernel while a system call does not
Both cost exactly the same because both end up in the kernel
A library call is an ordinary function inside your own address space with no privilege change and is cheap; a system call crosses into the kernel with a mode switch and costs far more
System calls are written in a high-level language while library calls are in assembly
questions.explanation: Library functions often wrap system calls — printf buffers in user space and eventually invokes the write system call.

questions.question: What is the difference between an interrupt, a trap and an exception?
options: All three are asynchronous signals from hardware devices
A trap comes from hardware while an interrupt comes from software
Exceptions are intentional while traps are accidental

A hardware interrupt is asynchronous and comes from a device; a trap is a synchronous, intentional software interrupt used to enter the kernel; an exception is a synchronous but unintended error such as divide-by-zero or a page fault
questions.explanation: The synchronous/asynchronous and intentional/unintended axes are what separate the three.

questions.question: What does DMA (Direct Memory Access) achieve?
options: It lets a device controller transfer a whole block of data to or from memory without the CPU copying each byte, interrupting the CPU only when the transfer completes
It gives a process direct access to another process's memory
It maps virtual addresses to physical addresses in hardware
It compresses data before writing it to disk
questions.explanation: Cycle stealing is how the DMA controller takes over the memory bus for occasional cycles while the CPU is not using it.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a hypervisor and a container?
options: Containers run a full guest OS while hypervisors share the host kernel
A hypervisor virtualizes the hardware so each VM runs a full guest OS; a container virtualizes the OS — all containers share the host kernel, isolated by namespaces and cgroups
Both share the host kernel and differ only in tooling
Hypervisors start in milliseconds while containers take minutes
questions.explanation: Containers are far lighter and start in milliseconds; VMs give stronger isolation and can run a different OS entirely.

questions.question: What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is running while a process is stored on disk
They are the same thing at different stages of compilation
A program is a passive set of instructions on disk; a process is a program in execution with its own memory, registers, stack, heap, open files and a PCB
One process can contain many programs
questions.explanation: One program can be running as many separate processes at once — each with independent state.

questions.question: Which transition correctly describes a process moving from Running to Ready?
options: It requested I/O and must wait for the device
It finished execution and was terminated
Preemption — its time quantum expired or a higher-priority process arrived
It was created and admitted into memory
questions.explanation: Running → Waiting is an I/O request; Waiting → Ready is I/O completion; Ready → Running is dispatch. The five states are New, Ready, Running, Waiting and Terminated.

questions.question: What does the Process Control Block (PCB) contain?
options: Only the process ID and its current state
Process ID, state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory management info, accounting data and the list of open files
The full source code of the running program
The physical memory addresses of every other process
questions.explanation: The PCB is exactly what gets saved and restored during a context switch — it is the OS's complete record of a process.

questions.question: Which two sections of a process's memory grow toward each other?
options: Text and Data
Data and BSS
Text and BSS
Heap (grows upward) and Stack (grows downward), into the free gap between them
questions.explanation: Text holds read-only compiled instructions, Data holds initialized globals, BSS holds uninitialized globals, Heap holds dynamic allocations and Stack holds locals and return addresses.

questions.question: Why is a thread called a lightweight process?
options: Because it has its own program counter, registers and stack, but shares the code, data, heap and open files with every other thread in the process
Because it uses less CPU time than a process
Because it can only run short-lived tasks
Because it has no state of its own at all
questions.explanation: A thread is the smallest unit of CPU scheduling — a single sequential flow of control inside a process.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
options: Threads have isolated address spaces while processes share memory
Processes are cheaper to create and switch than threads

A process is heavyweight with its own isolated address space and needs IPC to communicate; a thread is lightweight, shares its parent's address space, and is far cheaper to create and switch — but a crashing thread can bring down the whole process
Only processes can run on multiple cores
questions.explanation: Shared memory is exactly why threads need synchronization while separate processes do not.

questions.question: What are the benefits of multithreading?
options: It eliminates the need for any synchronization
It guarantees a program will never deadlock
It removes the need for the OS scheduler
Responsiveness, free resource sharing through shared memory, economy since threads are cheap to create and switch, and scalability across multiple cores
questions.explanation: The cost is synchronization complexity, race conditions and much harder debugging.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of user-level threads?
options: They are slower to switch than kernel-level threads
The kernel does not know they exist, so one blocking system call blocks every thread in the process and they cannot use multiple cores
They require special hardware support
They cannot share memory with each other
questions.explanation: Kernel-level threads are heavier to create and switch, but a blocked thread does not stall the others and they run truly in parallel.

questions.question: What is context switching, and why is it costly?
options: Saving the current process's state into its PCB and loading the next one's — it is pure overhead since no useful work happens during the switch
Moving a process from disk into main memory
Changing a process's scheduling priority at runtime
Translating a virtual address into a physical address
questions.explanation: This is exactly why a too-small time quantum in Round Robin destroys performance — switching dominates real work.

questions.question: Why is a process context switch more expensive than a thread context switch?
options: Because processes have more registers to save
Because a process switch must also change the memory map, flushing the TLB and often invalidating cache, whereas a thread switch keeps the address space and page tables valid
Because thread switches are done entirely in hardware
Because a process switch must write the entire heap to disk
questions.explanation: A thread switch within one process only swaps registers, the program counter and the stack pointer.

questions.question: What is a zombie process?
options: A process that consumes CPU without producing output
A process whose parent has died and been adopted by init
A process that has finished executing but whose entry remains in the process table because the parent has not called wait() to read its exit status
A process stuck waiting on a lock held by another
questions.explanation: A zombie holds no memory, just a table slot. An orphan is the opposite — still running, but its parent died and init/systemd adopts it.

questions.question: What are the two models of Inter-Process Communication?
options: Synchronous and asynchronous signalling only
Polling and interrupt-driven communication
Blocking and non-blocking file access
Shared memory (fastest — processes read/write a common region directly but must synchronize themselves) and message passing (kernel-mediated, safer, and works across machines)
questions.explanation: Mechanisms include pipes, named pipes (FIFOs), message queues, shared memory, semaphores, signals and sockets.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a pipe and a socket?
options: A pipe is a unidirectional channel between processes on the same machine; a socket is a bidirectional endpoint identified by IP address and port that also works across machines over a network
A socket works only between related processes while a pipe works between any two
Pipes are bidirectional and sockets are unidirectional
Both work only within a single process
questions.explanation: An ordinary pipe works only between related processes; a named pipe (FIFO) exists in the file system and works between unrelated ones.

questions.question: What is copy-on-write in the context of fork()?
options: The child's memory is fully duplicated immediately at fork time
The parent's memory is written to disk before the child starts
Parent and child initially share the same physical pages marked read-only, and a private copy is made only when one of them actually writes
The child writes to the parent's memory directly with no copy at all
questions.explanation: This makes fork nearly free, which matters because the child usually calls exec() and discards the old image anyway.

questions.question: What are the goals of CPU scheduling?
options: Maximize CPU utilization and throughput, minimize turnaround, waiting and response times, and keep allocation fair with no starvation
Minimize the amount of RAM each process consumes
Guarantee that every process finishes in the same amount of time
Eliminate the need for context switching
questions.explanation: Some goals conflict — optimizing throughput can hurt response time — which is why different algorithms make different trade-offs.

questions.question: Which scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming?
options: The short-term (CPU) scheduler
The long-term (job) scheduler, which decides which jobs are admitted into memory
The medium-term scheduler
The dispatcher
questions.explanation: The short-term scheduler picks which ready process runs next and must be fast; the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out to relieve memory pressure.

questions.question: Which pair of algorithms is preemptive?
options: FCFS and plain SJF
FCFS and Round Robin
Round Robin and SRTF
SJF and HRRN
questions.explanation: Preemptive scheduling lets the OS forcibly take the CPU back on quantum expiry or a higher-priority arrival — necessary for time-sharing.

questions.question: What is the difference between the scheduler and the dispatcher?
options: The dispatcher decides the policy while the scheduler executes it
Both terms describe the same kernel module
The scheduler runs in user mode while the dispatcher runs in kernel mode
The scheduler decides which process should run next (the policy); the dispatcher performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps to the right instruction (the mechanism)
questions.explanation: Dispatch latency is the time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another — pure overhead that should be minimal.

questions.question: What is the convoy effect in FCFS scheduling?
options: One long CPU-bound process at the head of the queue makes all the short I/O-bound processes wait behind it, leaving devices idle and hurting throughput
Several processes arrive at exactly the same instant and deadlock
Processes are grouped into convoys and scheduled as a batch
The CPU alternates rapidly between two processes and makes no progress
questions.explanation: FCFS runs processes in arrival order, non-preemptively — simple and fair in intent, but with poor average waiting time.

questions.question: Why is SJF impossible to implement perfectly?
options: Because it requires preemption, which most systems lack
Because the CPU burst length must be predicted in advance — usually by exponential averaging of past bursts
Because it always causes deadlock
Because it cannot be combined with any other algorithm
questions.explanation: SJF is provably optimal for minimum average waiting time, but both it and its preemptive form SRTF can starve long processes.

questions.question: What happens if the Round Robin time quantum is set too small?
options: The algorithm degenerates into FCFS
Processes begin to starve indefinitely
Context-switch overhead dominates and very little real work gets done
The scheduler can no longer preempt any process
questions.explanation: A quantum that is too large degenerates into FCFS. The rule of thumb is that the quantum should exceed about 80% of CPU bursts.

questions.question: What is the fatal flaw of priority scheduling, and how is it fixed?
options: It cannot be made preemptive; the fix is Round Robin
It requires knowing burst times in advance; the fix is exponential averaging
It causes deadlock; the fix is the Banker's algorithm
Indefinite blocking, where low-priority processes may starve; the fix is aging, which raises a process's priority the longer it waits
questions.explanation: Priorities may be internal (memory needs, burst time) or external (importance, funds), and the algorithm exists in preemptive and non-preemptive forms.

questions.question: What is aging in the context of scheduling?
options: Gradually increasing the priority of a process the longer it waits, so even the lowest-priority job eventually runs
Removing processes that have been in memory too long
Reducing the time quantum as the system load rises
Terminating a process that exceeds its allotted CPU time
questions.explanation: Aging is the standard cure for starvation — indefinite blocking caused by higher-priority processes continually arriving.

questions.question: How does Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) scheduling differ from a plain Multilevel Queue?
options: MLFQ uses a single queue while multilevel queue uses several
MLFQ allows processes to move between queues — demoted when they use a full quantum (marking them CPU-bound) and promoted by aging — whereas in a plain multilevel queue a process never changes queue
MLFQ requires knowing each process's burst time in advance
MLFQ is non-preemptive while multilevel queue is preemptive
questions.explanation: That movement automatically favours short, interactive jobs without ever needing to know burst times in advance.

questions.question: How is waiting time calculated in scheduling numericals?
options: Waiting time = Completion time − Arrival time
Waiting time = Burst time − Arrival time
Waiting time = Turnaround time − Burst time
Waiting time = Arrival time + Burst time
questions.explanation: Turnaround = Completion − Arrival, Waiting = Turnaround − Burst, and Response = first CPU allocation − Arrival. These formulas drive every Gantt-chart question.

questions.question: How does HRRN scheduling avoid starvation?
options: By preempting any process that runs longer than one quantum
By running the shortest job first at all times
By using a fixed round-robin rotation
It picks the highest response ratio = (waiting time + burst time) / burst time, so a long job's ratio keeps rising as it waits until it eventually wins
questions.explanation: HRRN gets much of SJF's throughput benefit while structurally preventing the starvation SJF suffers from.

questions.question: Why is process synchronization needed?
options: Because concurrent processes sharing data can corrupt it — the final result would otherwise depend on the unpredictable order of execution
Because the CPU cannot run more than one process at a time
Because processes must be started in a fixed alphabetical order
Because memory allocation requires it
questions.explanation: Synchronization enforces that shared data is touched by one thread at a time — the classic failure is a lost update on a shared counter.

questions.question: Why is count++ unsafe when two threads execute it concurrently?
options: Because the compiler refuses to generate code for it
Because it is really load-increment-store, so if two threads interleave those three steps one increment is silently lost
Because integers cannot be shared between threads
Because it always causes a deadlock
questions.explanation: This is the textbook race condition — the outcome depends on the timing of the interleaving, and the fix is to make the critical section mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Which three requirements must any solution to the critical section problem satisfy?
options: Atomicity, Consistency and Durability
Preemption, Aging and Fairness
Mutual Exclusion, Progress and Bounded Waiting
Locking, Signalling and Blocking
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion allows at most one process inside; progress prevents indefinite postponement of the choice; bounded waiting is what rules out starvation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a binary and a counting semaphore?
options: A binary semaphore can exceed 1 while a counting semaphore cannot
Binary semaphores are for signalling and counting semaphores for locking only
Both take only the values 0 and 1 and differ only in name
A binary semaphore takes only 0 or 1 and acts like a lock for one resource; a counting semaphore can exceed 1 and tracks a pool of N identical resources, blocking when it reaches 0
questions.explanation: A semaphore is an integer accessed only through the atomic operations wait() and signal().

questions.question: What does the wait(S) operation do?
options: It decrements S, and if S becomes negative the process blocks and joins S's waiting queue
It increments S and wakes a waiting process
It sets S to zero unconditionally
It busy-waits until S becomes positive without blocking
questions.explanation: signal(S) increments S and wakes one waiting process. Both must execute atomically, or the semaphore itself becomes a race condition.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
options: A semaphore can only be used by two processes while a mutex supports many
A mutex has ownership — only the thread that locked it may unlock it, and it protects exactly one resource; a semaphore is a signalling mechanism with no ownership that can admit N processes
A mutex can admit N processes while a semaphore admits only one
Mutexes are implemented in hardware and semaphores in software
questions.explanation: Use a mutex for mutual exclusion over a shared variable; use a semaphore to signal between processes or manage a resource pool.

questions.question: What is a monitor?
options: A hardware device that watches CPU utilization
A kernel thread that detects deadlocks
A high-level language construct bundling shared data with the procedures that operate on it, guaranteeing only one process is active inside at a time
A special semaphore that can never reach zero
questions.explanation: Java's synchronized and C#'s lock implement this. It is safer than raw semaphores because the compiler enforces mutual exclusion — you cannot forget to release.

questions.question: What does Peterson's solution use to coordinate two processes?
options: Two counting semaphores and a mutex
A hardware test-and-set instruction
A single shared integer counter
A shared boolean array flag[2] indicating intent to enter, plus an integer turn indicating whose turn it is
questions.explanation: It is a pure software solution satisfying all three requirements, but it relies on atomic loads/stores and does not survive modern instruction reordering without memory barriers.

questions.question: What does bounded waiting guarantee?
options: That once a process requests entry to its critical section, only a bounded number of other processes may enter before it does
That a process will never be preempted while inside its critical section
That the critical section executes within a fixed number of CPU cycles
That at most two processes may be inside the critical section at once
questions.explanation: Without it a process could wait forever even while the algorithm technically makes progress — bounded waiting is precisely what rules out starvation.

questions.question: When is a spinlock actually a good choice?
options: On a single-CPU system, where it avoids scheduler overhead
On a multiprocessor when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of two context switches — which is why kernels use them for very short critical sections
Whenever the critical section performs disk I/O
Never — spinlocks are always worse than blocking locks
questions.explanation: Busy waiting burns CPU cycles achieving nothing, so it is wasteful on a single CPU where the holder cannot run concurrently anyway.

questions.question: Which classical synchronization problem is the textbook illustration of deadlock and starvation?
options: The Producer-Consumer (bounded buffer) problem
The Readers-Writers problem
The Dining Philosophers problem — five philosophers competing for five shared forks
The Sleeping Barber problem
questions.explanation: Producer-Consumer models a bounded buffer with two counting semaphores plus a mutex; Readers-Writers allows concurrent readers but exclusive writers; Sleeping Barber models limited-capacity queues.

questions.question: What is priority inversion, and how is it fixed?
options: A low-priority task is promoted above a high-priority one by the scheduler; the fix is disabling aging
Two tasks swap priorities each time they are preempted; the fix is a fixed priority table
The scheduler reverses the priority queue on each quantum; the fix is FIFO ordering
A high-priority task is blocked on a lock held by a low-priority task while a medium-priority task preempts the low one; fixed by priority inheritance or a priority ceiling
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder to the waiter's priority. This bug famously nearly ended the Mars Pathfinder mission.

questions.question: What is a deadlock?
options: A state where a set of processes are each blocked forever, waiting for a resource held by another process in the same set
A process that runs indefinitely without releasing the CPU
A process that is runnable but never scheduled
A situation where two threads write the same variable simultaneously
questions.explanation: The classic example: P1 holds the printer and wants the scanner while P2 holds the scanner and wants the printer.

questions.question: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability
Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption and Circular Wait
Starvation, Livelock, Blocking and Waiting
Preemption, Aging, Priority and Fairness
questions.explanation: These are the Coffman conditions and all four must hold simultaneously — breaking any single one makes deadlock impossible.

questions.question: Which deadlock-handling strategy do Windows and Linux actually use in practice?
options: Deadlock prevention through strict resource ordering
Deadlock avoidance using the Banker's algorithm
Ignoring the problem — the Ostrich algorithm — because deadlocks are rare and prevention is expensive
Continuous detection with automatic rollback
questions.explanation: The four approaches are prevention, avoidance, detection with recovery, and ignoring it. General-purpose OSes choose the last.

questions.question: Which deadlock prevention technique is the most practical in real code?
options: Requiring every process to request all its resources up front
Making all resources shareable so mutual exclusion never applies
Forcibly preempting resources from any waiting process
Imposing a global ordering on resource types and requiring requests in increasing order, which breaks circular wait
questions.explanation: Requiring everything up front causes low utilization and starvation; not all resources can be made shareable; preemption is impossible for many resource types.

questions.question: How does the Banker's algorithm work?
options: It maintains Available, Max, Allocation and Need matrices, pretends to grant each request, and runs a safety check to find a sequence in which every process can finish — denying the request if no such sequence exists
It detects cycles in a wait-for graph and kills the cheapest victim
It orders all resources numerically and enforces increasing-order requests
It periodically restarts all blocked processes
questions.explanation: It is called Banker's because a bank never allocates cash such that it could not satisfy all its customers. It requires knowing each process's maximum claim in advance.

questions.question: What does it mean for a system to be in an unsafe state?
options: Deadlock has definitely already occurred
No safe sequence exists, so the OS can no longer guarantee it can prevent deadlock — though deadlock may still not happen
All resources have been allocated and none remain
At least one process has been aborted
questions.explanation: A safe state guarantees no deadlock; an unsafe state merely removes that guarantee. Safe ⊂ unsafe ⊂ deadlock is the wrong way round — deadlock states are a subset of unsafe states.

questions.question: In a resource allocation graph with multiple instances per resource type, what does a cycle indicate?
options: Deadlock has definitely occurred
The graph is malformed and must be redrawn
A cycle is only a necessary condition — deadlock may or may not exist, so the detection algorithm must be run
No deadlock is possible
questions.explanation: With exactly one instance per resource type, a cycle does mean deadlock. Multiple instances break that guarantee.

questions.question: What must victim selection avoid during deadlock recovery?
options: Choosing a process that holds no resources
Choosing a process with the highest priority
Choosing more than one process at a time
Always picking the same process, which would cause starvation
questions.explanation: Selection weighs priority, how long the process has run and how many resources it holds. Recovery options are aborting processes or preempting resources and rolling back.

questions.question: What is the difference between deadlock, starvation and livelock?
options: Deadlock: processes are blocked forever in a circular wait. Starvation: a process is runnable but the scheduler keeps passing it over. Livelock: processes are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress
All three describe the same blocked condition
Livelock means blocked while deadlock means running
Starvation occurs only in single-threaded programs
questions.explanation: Deadlock = blocked forever; livelock = busy forever with no progress; starvation = runnable but never scheduled.

questions.question: Why do general-purpose operating systems adopt the Ostrich algorithm?
options: Because deadlock detection is mathematically impossible
Because deadlocks are infrequent, prevention and avoidance cost significant performance and flexibility, and killing a hung process or rebooting is acceptable to users
Because their kernels have no concept of shared resources
Because the hardware prevents deadlock automatically
questions.explanation: It is a deliberate engineering trade-off, not an oversight — the cost of the cure exceeds the cost of the disease for typical desktop and server workloads.

questions.question: Which of these is a goal of memory management?
options: Eliminating the need for secondary storage entirely
Guaranteeing every process an equal amount of RAM
Relocation, protection, sharing, logical organization and physical organization — while maximizing the degree of multiprogramming for a given amount of RAM
Ensuring processes are always loaded at the same physical address
questions.explanation: Relocation means a process can be swapped out and returned to a different address, which is exactly why fixed physical addresses would be a problem.

questions.question: What does the MMU do?
options: It allocates heap memory when a program calls malloc
It hardware-translates the CPU-generated logical (virtual) address into the real physical address at run time, by walking the page table or adding a relocation register
It decides which process runs next on the CPU
It compresses memory pages before writing them to disk
questions.explanation: The program never sees a physical address — that indirection is precisely what makes relocation and inter-process protection possible.

questions.question: Which type of address binding do modern systems use, and why?
options: Compile-time binding, because it is fastest
Load-time binding, because it needs no hardware
Link-time binding, because it resolves all symbols early
Execution-time binding, because deferring the mapping until run time lets the process move around in memory — which requires MMU hardware
questions.explanation: Compile-time binding bakes absolute addresses in, forcing the program to load at a known location; load-time binding fixes them when loaded.

questions.question: Which contiguous allocation strategy performs worst in practice?
options: Worst fit — it takes the largest hole, and although the remainder is usable it gives the poorest utilization overall
First fit, because it scans from the beginning every time
Best fit, because it leaves tiny fragments
All three perform identically
questions.explanation: First fit is the fastest; best fit wastes least per allocation but leaves many tiny unusable fragments. Both beat worst fit on speed and utilization.

questions.question: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
options: Internal fragmentation is caused by variable-size allocation and external by fixed-size allocation

Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated block (caused by fixed-size allocation such as paging); external fragmentation is free memory split into scattered small holes so a large request fails despite enough total free space (caused by variable-size allocation)
Both mean the same thing measured at different levels
External fragmentation occurs only on disk, never in RAM
questions.explanation: Paging eliminates external fragmentation but introduces internal fragmentation in the last page; compaction cures external fragmentation in segmented systems.

questions.question: Why is compaction only possible with execution-time address binding?
options: Because compaction requires the process to be swapped to disk first
Because only execution-time binding uses a page table
Because compaction physically moves processes to new addresses, which only works if their addresses are resolved at run time rather than fixed earlier
Because compile-time binding does not allow multiprogramming
questions.explanation: Compaction shuffles allocated blocks so free holes merge into one contiguous region. It is expensive because everything must be copied.

questions.question: What is swapping?
options: Exchanging the contents of two registers during a context switch
Replacing one page in memory with another from disk
Rotating processes through the ready queue in round-robin order
Temporarily moving an entire process out of main memory to a backing store on disk and bringing it back later
questions.explanation: Swapping lets total memory demand exceed physical RAM and raises the degree of multiprogramming, at the cost of high transfer time. Modern systems swap pages rather than whole processes.

questions.question: What problem does paging solve?
options: It eliminates external fragmentation, because logical memory is split into fixed-size pages that can go into any free physical frame with no need for contiguous allocation
It eliminates internal fragmentation completely
It removes the need for a page table
It guarantees that every process fits entirely in RAM
questions.explanation: The costs are internal fragmentation in the last page and the extra memory access needed to consult the page table.

questions.question: What is the key difference between paging and segmentation?
options: Paging uses variable-size blocks while segmentation uses fixed-size blocks
Paging uses fixed-size blocks invisible to the programmer and managed by the OS; segmentation uses variable-size blocks that match the programmer's logical view (code, stack, heap)
Both use fixed-size blocks and differ only in table structure
Segmentation suffers internal fragmentation while paging suffers external fragmentation
questions.explanation: Paging suffers internal fragmentation and needs a page table; segmentation suffers external fragmentation and needs a segment table. Many systems combine both.

questions.question: What is dynamic loading?
options: Loading the entire program into memory before execution begins
Loading a program from a network location rather than local disk
Deferring the loading of a routine until it is actually called, so unused code such as rare error handlers never consumes memory
Increasing the size of the heap while the program runs
questions.explanation: Dynamic linking defers library binding to run time so one shared copy serves all processes. Overlays were the old manual technique for running a program larger than RAM.

questions.question: What is virtual memory?
options: A technique letting a process execute even when it is not entirely in main memory, by keeping the rest on disk behind a logical address space
A faster type of RAM installed alongside main memory
A region of the disk reserved exclusively for the kernel
A cache that stores recently used page-table entries
questions.explanation: Advantages: programs can exceed physical memory, more processes fit so CPU utilization rises, less I/O is needed to load a process, and processes stay isolated.

questions.question: What is demand paging?
options: Loading the entire process into memory before it starts
The lazy-loading implementation of virtual memory — a page is brought in only when it is actually referenced, never in advance
Requesting extra pages from the user when memory runs low
Writing every modified page back to disk immediately
questions.explanation: Pages not in memory are marked invalid; touching one triggers a page fault that fetches it. This cuts startup time sharply since most programs never touch most of their code.

questions.question: What happens when a page fault occurs?
options: The process is terminated with a segmentation fault
The page is silently skipped and execution continues
The OS checks the reference is legal, finds a free frame or evicts one, reads the page from disk, updates the page table and restarts the faulting instruction
The CPU switches permanently to another process
questions.explanation: A page fault costs milliseconds against nanoseconds for a memory access, which is why the fault rate dominates virtual-memory performance.

questions.question: How does the TLB improve performance?
options: It compresses page-table entries to save memory
It stores the pages themselves rather than their addresses
It prefetches pages before they are referenced
It is a small fast hardware cache of recent page-to-frame translations, so on a hit the physical address is formed with no extra memory access
questions.explanation: Without it every memory reference needs two accesses — one for the page table, one for the data. Locality gives hit rates of 90-99%.

questions.question: What is the formula for effective access time with a page fault rate p?
options: EAT = (1 − p) × memory_access_time + p × page_fault_service_time
EAT = p × memory_access_time + (1 − p) × page_fault_service_time
EAT = memory_access_time × page_fault_service_time
EAT = memory_access_time + p
questions.explanation: With 100 ns access and 8 ms fault service, a fault rate of just 1 in 1000 makes effective access roughly 8 microseconds — about 80× slower.

questions.question: What is thrashing, and what makes it self-worsening?
options: The disk head oscillating between distant tracks; it worsens as the queue grows
Two processes repeatedly preempting each other; it worsens with more CPUs
The system spends more time servicing page faults than executing, so CPU utilization collapses — and the OS, seeing low utilization, admits MORE processes and makes it worse
Memory becoming fragmented over time; it worsens with each allocation
questions.explanation: The cause is too high a degree of multiprogramming, leaving each process too few frames to hold its working set. Fixes: working set model, page-fault frequency control, or more RAM.

questions.question: What is the working set model?
options: The set of processes currently in the ready queue
The set of pages a process has referenced in the most recent Δ references — an approximation of its locality, used to decide how many frames it needs
The set of frames reserved permanently for the kernel
The set of pages modified since the last disk write
questions.explanation: If the total working set size of all processes exceeds available frames, the OS suspends a process to prevent thrashing.

questions.question: Why can the Optimal (OPT) page replacement algorithm not be implemented?
options: It requires more memory than any real system has
It only works with fixed-size pages
It is patented and cannot be used freely
It evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future, which requires knowledge of the future — so it serves only as a benchmark
questions.explanation: FIFO evicts the oldest-loaded page and suffers Belady's anomaly; LRU approximates Optimal using locality, and real systems use cheap approximations like the clock algorithm.

questions.question: Why does Belady's anomaly occur in FIFO but never in LRU?
options: Because FIFO is not a stack algorithm — the set of pages held with n frames is not guaranteed to be a subset of the set held with n+1 frames, whereas LRU and Optimal do have that subset property
Because FIFO uses more memory per entry than LRU
Because LRU never evicts any page
Because FIFO requires hardware support that LRU does not
questions.explanation: Belady's anomaly is the counter-intuitive result where adding more page frames increases the number of page faults.

questions.question: What is the trade-off when choosing a larger page size?
options: Larger pages reduce both internal fragmentation and page-table size
Larger pages give a smaller page table, better TLB coverage and fewer faults on sequential access — but more internal fragmentation and more wasted I/O
Larger pages always improve performance with no downside
Larger pages eliminate the need for a TLB
questions.explanation: A page is a block of logical memory and a frame is the identically-sized physical block it loads into. There is no universally best size; 4 KB is typical.

questions.question: What is spatial locality?
options: A recently used memory location is likely to be used again soon
Memory locations near a recently used one are likely to be accessed next, as in array traversal or sequential code
Two processes access the same memory region at the same time
A page stays in memory for a fixed period after being loaded
questions.explanation: Temporal locality is the repeat-access property (loop counters). Every cache, TLB and page replacement policy exists because locality holds.

questions.question: What is the advantage of an inverted page table?
options: It allows each process to have its own private table
It removes the need for a TLB entirely
Its size depends on the amount of physical RAM rather than on the number of processes, since it holds one entry per frame instead of per page
It makes page sharing between processes easier
questions.explanation: The trade-off is slower searching and difficult page sharing. Multilevel paging pages the page table itself; hashed page tables suit very large address spaces.

questions.question: How does the OS structurally prevent one process from reading another's memory?
options: By encrypting each process's pages with a unique key
By scanning every memory access in software before allowing it
By running each process on a dedicated CPU core
Each process has its own page table, so its virtual addresses simply cannot name another process's frames — and permission bits in page-table entries trap any violation
questions.explanation: Only kernel mode can modify these tables, and a violation raises a hardware trap the kernel turns into a segmentation fault.

questions.question: What does a file system do?
options: It organizes data on secondary storage into named files and directories, defining how they are stored, accessed and protected, and tracking metadata and free space
It manages which process gets the CPU next
It translates virtual addresses into physical addresses
It handles communication between processes on different machines
questions.explanation: Examples are NTFS, ext4, FAT32 and APFS. Basic operations: create, open, read, write, append, seek, truncate, rename, close and delete.

questions.question: What does an inode store — and what does it NOT store?
options: It stores the filename and the file's contents but not its permissions
It stores size, permissions, owner, timestamps, link count and pointers to data blocks — but NOT the filename, which lives in the directory entry
It stores only the pointers to data blocks and nothing else
It stores the directory hierarchy for the whole file system
questions.explanation: That separation of name from metadata is exactly what makes hard links possible — several directory entries can point at one inode.

questions.question: What is the difference between a hard link and a soft (symbolic) link?
options: A hard link contains a path string while a soft link points to an inode
Both point to the same inode and differ only in syntax

A hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode and cannot cross file systems; a soft link is a small file containing a path, which can cross file systems but breaks if the target is deleted
Soft links cannot be created for directories
questions.explanation: A file survives until its last hard link is deleted. A soft link whose target disappears becomes a dangling link.

questions.question: Which file allocation method supports direct access without causing external fragmentation?
options: Contiguous allocation
Linked allocation
No method achieves both
Indexed allocation, where an index block holds all the block pointers
questions.explanation: Contiguous gives excellent access but causes external fragmentation and cannot grow easily; linked avoids fragmentation but makes direct access impossible. Indexed costs index-block overhead for small files.

questions.question: What is the advantage of a bit vector for free space management?
options: One bit per block makes it simple and makes finding contiguous runs easy — though the whole map must stay in memory for speed
It uses no memory at all because it is stored only on disk
It allows blocks to be allocated without any bookkeeping
It automatically defragments the disk
questions.explanation: The alternative is a linked list of free blocks, which wastes no space but is slow to traverse. Grouping and counting are optimizations on that idea.

questions.question: Which file access method do databases most depend on?
options: Sequential access, reading one record after another in order
Direct (random) access, jumping straight to any block number
Batch access, processing all records at once
Streaming access, reading continuously without seeking
questions.explanation: Sequential access is what tapes forced and remains the most common; indexed access searches an index file first and then jumps, as in ISAM-style systems.

questions.question: How does C-SCAN differ from SCAN disk scheduling?
options: C-SCAN services requests in arrival order while SCAN sorts them
C-SCAN reverses at the last request while SCAN goes to the physical end
C-SCAN sweeps in one direction only and then jumps back to the start without servicing on the way, which gives more uniform wait times than SCAN's back-and-forth sweep
C-SCAN always picks the closest request next
questions.explanation: SSTF picks the closest request but can starve far ones; LOOK and C-LOOK behave like SCAN and C-SCAN but reverse at the last request rather than the disk edge.

questions.question: Which component of disk access time can disk scheduling actually reduce?
options: Rotational latency, by predicting sector positions
Transfer time, by compressing the data
Controller overhead, by batching commands
Seek time — the arm movement to the correct track, which is the largest component
questions.explanation: Rotational latency averages half a rotation and transfer time depends on data size. On SSDs seek and rotational latency vanish, so disk scheduling matters far less.

questions.question: Which RAID level provides striping with distributed parity, surviving one disk failure?
options: RAID 0
RAID 1
RAID 5
RAID 10
questions.explanation: RAID 0 is striping with no redundancy; RAID 1 is mirroring at 50% capacity cost; RAID 6 uses two parity blocks; RAID 10 is mirrored stripes. RAID is not a backup — it protects against disk failure, not deletion.
